## “The two sayings I have found most useful in life are these: responsibility, and delight.… What I speak of today as respect for one's work is responsibility; delight in one's work is interest. I deeply believe that a reasonable human life should be like this” — Liang Qichao

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“The two sayings I have found most useful in life are these: responsibility, and delight.… What I speak of today as respect for one's work is responsibility; delight in one's work is interest. I deeply believe that a reasonable human life should be like this.”

Chinese

“敬業與樂業”

The title of Liang Qichao's 1922 talk to students. The archive's English passage is a condensation of the talk's argument rather than a translation of one sentence, and it is marked as such with an ellipsis.

### Attribution notes

This is a speech, delivered at a school, and it has no single citable sentence behind the English rendering. Treating the condensed English as if it were a quotable line misrepresents its form: the interest of the passage is that Liang is arguing against the sharp division between work done for duty and work done for enjoyment, which is a position developed across a whole address.

#### About Liang Qichao

Liang Qichao (1873–1929) was a leading late-Qing and early-Republican intellectual who introduced Western political ideas and reshaped Chinese historiography and public opinion.

### How to read this passage

Philosophical debates cover free will, blame, collective responsibility, and duties to distant others. Technology and AI revive the question of who is accountable when systems act. This passage enters that discussion through responsibility.
